# 📚 LESSON 22: Handling Popups, Frames, Alerts & Tabs!

> 🎯 **Today's Goal:** Learn how to handle special browser scenarios that appear in real websites!
> ⏰ **Estimated Time:** 1 - 1.5 hours

---

## 💡 Simple Explanation — Why Do We Need This?

Real websites have special elements that appear OUTSIDE the normal page:

```
Normal page  → page.click(), page.fill() handles it ✅

Special cases:
→ Alert popup    → "Are you sure you want to delete?"
→ New tab opens  → clicked link opens new browser tab
→ iframe         → a page inside another page
→ File dialog    → upload file popup
```

> 💡 These need special Playwright handling — can't use normal locators!

---

## 🌍 Real-World Analogy: Unexpected Visitors 🚪

```
You're working at your desk (main page):

Suddenly:
→ Phone rings (alert popup) → you answer it!
→ Someone knocks on door (new tab) → you open it!
→ You look through a window (iframe) → different view!

Each unexpected visitor needs DIFFERENT handling!
Same in Playwright — each special case needs different code!
```

---

## 🔷 TYPE 1: Browser Alerts (Dialogs)

Alerts are the popup boxes that appear on screen:

```
Types of alerts:
→ Alert    → just shows message, only OK button
→ Confirm  → shows message, OK and Cancel buttons
→ Prompt   → asks for input, text field + OK/Cancel
```

### 🌍 Analogy: A Door Bell 🔔

```
Alert   = Doorbell rings, you just acknowledge it (OK)
Confirm = Delivery man asks "Sign here?" (OK/Cancel)
Prompt  = Someone asks "What's your name?" (type + OK)
```

### How to Handle Alerts in Playwright:

```typescript
// Set up listener BEFORE action that triggers alert:
page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => {
    console.log(`Alert message: ${dialog.message()}`);
    await dialog.accept();    // Click OK
    // OR:
    await dialog.dismiss();   // Click Cancel
});

// Now trigger the alert:
await page.click('#deleteButton');
// Alert appears → listener handles it automatically!
```

> ⚠️ **IMPORTANT RULE:**
> Set up the listener BEFORE the action that triggers it!
> Otherwise alert appears and Playwright doesn't know what to do!

---

## 💻 Code Example 1: Handling Alerts

Create `alerts.spec.ts`:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Handle Alert Demo', async ({ page }) => {

    // Go to a page that has alerts
    await page.goto('https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/javascript_alerts');
    console.log('✅ Navigated to alerts page');

    // HANDLE SIMPLE ALERT:
    // Step 1: Set up listener BEFORE clicking!
    page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => {
        console.log(`Alert type: ${dialog.type()}`);
        console.log(`Alert message: ${dialog.message()}`);
        await dialog.accept();    // Click OK!
    });

    // Step 2: Click button that triggers alert:
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Click for JS Alert' }).click();
    console.log('✅ Alert handled successfully!');

    // Verify result:
    await expect(page.locator('#result')).toHaveText('You successfuly clicked an alert');
    console.log('✅ Result verified!');
});
```

---

## 🔷 TYPE 2: New Tabs

When clicking a link opens a NEW browser tab — normal locators won't work on the new tab!

### 🌍 Analogy: Opening a New Office Door 🚪

```
You're in Office 1 (main page)
You click a link → Office 2 opens (new tab)

To work in Office 2:
→ You need to WALK to Office 2 (switch to new page)
→ THEN do your work there
→ You can switch back to Office 1 anytime!
```

### How to Handle New Tabs:

```typescript
// Wait for new page AND click link together:
const [newPage] = await Promise.all([
    page.context().waitForEvent('page'),  // Wait for new tab!
    page.click('#openNewTab')             // Click that opens new tab
]);

// Now work on the new tab:
await newPage.waitForLoadState();
console.log('New tab title:', await newPage.title());

// Do things on new tab:
await newPage.locator('#element').click();

// Close new tab when done:
await newPage.close();

// Back to original page automatically!
```

---

## 💻 Code Example 2: Handling New Tabs

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Handle New Tab Demo', async ({ page }) => {

    await page.goto('https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/windows');
    console.log('✅ Navigated to page');

    // Click link that opens new tab:
    const [newPage] = await Promise.all([
        page.context().waitForEvent('page'),
        page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Click Here' }).click()
    ]);

    // Wait for new page to load:
    await newPage.waitForLoadState();
    console.log('✅ New tab opened!');

    // Verify new tab content:
    await expect(newPage.getByRole('heading', { name: 'New Window' })).toBeVisible();
    console.log('✅ New tab content verified!');

    // Close new tab:
    await newPage.close();
    console.log('✅ New tab closed!');

    // We're back on original page:
    console.log('✅ Back on original page!');
});
```

---

## 🔷 TYPE 3: iFrames (Page Inside a Page)

An iframe is like a **window inside a webpage** — showing a different page!

### 🌍 Analogy: A TV Inside a Room 📺

```
Your room (main page)
TV screen (iframe) → shows completely different content!

To change TV channel (interact with iframe):
→ Pick up REMOTE for the TV (frameLocator)
→ THEN press buttons (interact with iframe elements)

Can't use room's light switch to change TV channel!
Need the TV's own remote! 🎯
```

### HTML Example:
```html
<!-- Main page has an iframe: -->
<iframe id="payment-frame" src="https://payment.com">
    <!-- Different content inside! -->
    <input id="card-number" type="text">
</iframe>
```

### How to Handle iFrames:

```typescript
// Get the frame locator first:
const frame = page.frameLocator('#payment-frame');
//                  ↑ like picking up the TV remote!

// Now interact WITH the frame:
await frame.locator('#card-number').fill('4111111111111111');
//   ↑ using frame's remote to interact!
```

---

## 💻 Code Example 3: Handling iFrames

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Handle iFrame Demo', async ({ page }) => {

    await page.goto('https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/iframe');
    console.log('✅ Navigated to iframe page');

    // Get the frame locator:
    const frame = page.frameLocator('#mce_0_ifr');
    console.log('✅ Frame located!');

    // Interact with element INSIDE the frame:
    await frame.locator('#tinymce').click();
    await frame.locator('#tinymce').fill('Hello from inside the iframe!');
    console.log('✅ Typed inside iframe!');

    // Verify text inside frame:
    await expect(frame.locator('#tinymce')).toContainText('Hello from inside');
    console.log('✅ iframe content verified!');
});
```

## 🔷 TYPE 4: File Upload Dialog

When you click "Upload" — a file picker dialog appears!

```typescript
// Handle file upload:
await page.locator('#fileInput').setInputFiles('path/to/file.pdf');
//                                ↑ No dialog needed!
//                                  Playwright handles it directly!

// Upload multiple files:
await page.locator('#fileInput').setInputFiles([
    'file1.pdf',
    'file2.pdf'
]);

// Clear file selection:
await page.locator('#fileInput').setInputFiles([]);
```

> 💡 `setInputFiles()` is special — it directly sets the file without opening a dialog!
> No need to interact with the OS file picker! 🎯

## 🔗 Connecting to Real Projects

```typescript
// In real e-commerce tests:

test('Complete Purchase with Special Scenarios', async ({ page }) => {

    // 1. Handle cookie consent popup (alert-like):
    page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => {
        await dialog.accept();
    });

    // 2. Navigate to product page:
    await page.goto('https://shop.com/product/123');

    // 3. Click "Pay Securely" → opens in iframe:
    const paymentFrame = page.frameLocator('#payment-iframe');
    await paymentFrame.locator('#card-number').fill('4111111111111111');

    // 4. Upload receipt document:
    await page.locator('#receipt-upload').setInputFiles('receipt.pdf');

    // 5. Click "View Order" → opens new tab:
    const [orderPage] = await Promise.all([
        page.context().waitForEvent('page'),
        page.click('#view-order')
    ]);

    await expect(orderPage.getByText('Order Confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});
```

## ⚠️ Common Mistakes Beginners Make

❌ **Mistake 1: Setting up dialog listener AFTER the trigger**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — too late! Alert already appeared!
await page.click('#deleteBtn');    // Alert appears here!
page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => {  // Too late! ❌
    await dialog.accept();
});

// ✅ CORRECT — listener set up BEFORE click!
page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => {  // Set up first! ✅
    await dialog.accept();
});
await page.click('#deleteBtn');    // Now alert appears → handled!
```

❌ **Mistake 2: Using normal locator inside iframe**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — can't find element inside iframe with page locator!
await page.locator('#card-number').fill('4111');
// Element not found! It's inside iframe!

// ✅ CORRECT — use frameLocator first!
const frame = page.frameLocator('#payment-frame');
await frame.locator('#card-number').fill('4111');
```

❌ **Mistake 3: Not waiting for new tab to load**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — new tab might not be ready!
const [newPage] = await Promise.all([...]);
await newPage.locator('#element').click();  // Too fast! 💥

// ✅ CORRECT — wait for load state first!
const [newPage] = await Promise.all([...]);
await newPage.waitForLoadState();           // Wait for load!
await newPage.locator('#element').click();  // Now safe! ✅
```

### Question 3: What does `Promise.all()` do?
> *"Though I am not that clear, promise.all catches and controls the newly opened tab"*

✅ **Honest answer — good that you said you're not fully clear!**

Let me explain it simply:

### 💡 What is `Promise.all()`?

```typescript
const [newPage] = await Promise.all([
    page.context().waitForEvent('page'),  // Promise 1: Listen for new tab
    page.click('#openTab')                // Promise 2: Click that opens tab
]);
```

> 🌍 **Analogy: A Photographer and an Event 📸**
> ```
> Photographer (Promise 1): "I'm ready to capture the moment!"
> Event happens (Promise 2): Someone clicks the button!
>
> Promise.all says:
> "START both at the SAME TIME!"
> "Wait until BOTH are done!"
> "THEN give me the results!"
> ```

> 💡 **Why both at same time?**
> ```
> ❌ If we listen AFTER clicking:
> Click happens → new tab opens → we start listening
> TOO LATE! We missed the new tab event!
>
> ✅ Promise.all starts BOTH simultaneously:
> Start listening AND click at same time!
> New tab opens → listener catches it immediately! ✅
> ```

```typescript
// Simple breakdown:
Promise.all([
    waitForNewTab,    // "Hey! Tell me when new tab opens!"
    clickTheButton    // "Now click the button!"
])
// Both happen at same time → new tab caught instantly!
```

### 🏆 Score: 6/10 — Honest answer! Now you know the full picture!

# 📚 LESSON 23: Test Fixtures!

> 🎯 **Today's Goal:** Understand what fixtures are and how they make tests cleaner and reusable!
> ⏰ **Estimated Time:** 1 - 1.5 hours

---

## 💡 Simple Explanation — The Problem First

Look at your current tests — what do they ALL have in common?

```typescript
// Test 1 — Login Test:
test('Login Test', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://practicetestautomation.com/practice-test-login/');
    await page.fill('#username', 'student');
    await page.fill('#password', 'Password123');
    await page.click('#submit');
    // actual test logic...
});

// Test 2 — Logout Test:
test('Logout Test', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://practicetestautomation.com/practice-test-login/');
    await page.fill('#username', 'student');
    await page.fill('#password', 'Password123');
    await page.click('#submit');
    // actual test logic...
});

// Test 3 — Dashboard Test:
test('Dashboard Test', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://practicetestautomation.com/practice-test-login/');
    await page.fill('#username', 'student');
    await page.fill('#password', 'Password123');
    await page.click('#submit');
    // actual test logic...
});
```

> 😱 The SAME login code is repeated in EVERY test!
> What if password changes? You update 100 test files!
> This is called **code duplication** — the enemy of good automation!

---

## 🌍 Real-World Analogy: A Hotel Room 🏨

```
Imagine staying at a hotel:

Without fixtures (bad):
→ Every morning you bring your own:
  - Towels
  - Soap
  - Shampoo
  - Bedsheets
  → Carry all this every single day! 😫

With fixtures (good):
→ Hotel PREPARES everything for you:
  - Room is cleaned ✅
  - Towels are fresh ✅
  - Soap is ready ✅
  → You just walk in and USE the room! 😊
```

> 💡 **Fixtures = the hotel that prepares everything before you arrive!**
> Your test just USES what's already prepared!

---

## 📝 What Are Fixtures?

Fixtures are **reusable setup code** that:

```
1. Run BEFORE your test (setup)
2. Give your test what it needs (provide)
3. Clean up AFTER your test (teardown)
```

```typescript
// WITHOUT fixture — setup repeated in every test!
test('Test 1', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('...');        // repeated!
    await page.fill('#username');  // repeated!
    await page.fill('#password');  // repeated!
    await page.click('#submit');   // repeated!
    // actual test...
});

// WITH fixture — setup done ONCE, used everywhere!
test('Test 1', async ({ loggedInPage }) => {
//                       ↑ Already logged in!
//                         No setup code needed!
    // actual test immediately!
});
```

---

## 🔍 Built-in Fixtures You Already Know!

Playwright comes with built-in fixtures you've been using!

```typescript
test('My Test', async ({ page, browser, context, request }) => {
//                        ↑      ↑         ↑        ↑
//                    Built-in fixtures from Playwright!
```

| Fixture | What It Provides |
|---------|-----------------|
| `page` | A fresh browser page |
| `browser` | The browser instance |
| `context` | Browser context (like incognito) |
| `request` | For API testing |

> 💡 Every time you write `async ({ page })` — you're using a fixture!
> Playwright creates a fresh page and gives it to your test!
> After test ends → Playwright closes the page automatically!

---

## 🔷 Creating Your OWN Custom Fixture!

This is the POWERFUL part — creating fixtures for YOUR needs!

### Step 1: Create a fixtures file

Create a new file `fixtures.ts` in your tests folder:

```typescript
// fixtures.ts

import { test as base, Page } from '@playwright/test';

// Define your custom fixture type:
type MyFixtures = {
    loggedInPage: Page;    // A page that's already logged in!
};

// Create custom test with fixture:
export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({

    // Define the loggedInPage fixture:
    loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {

        // SETUP — runs before each test:
        await page.goto('https://practicetestautomation.com/practice-test-login/');
        await page.locator('#username').fill('student');
        await page.locator('#password').fill('Password123');
        await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
        await page.waitForURL(/logged-in-successfully/);
        console.log('✅ Fixture: Logged in successfully!');

        // PROVIDE the page to the test:
        await use(page);
        //    ↑ Everything above = SETUP
        //    ↑ Everything below = TEARDOWN

        // TEARDOWN — runs after each test:
        await page.close();
        console.log('✅ Fixture: Page closed!');
    }
});

// Export expect too!
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

---

### Step 2: Use Your Fixture in Tests

Create `fixture.spec.ts`:

```typescript
// fixture.spec.ts

// Import from YOUR fixtures file, not playwright!
import { test, expect } from './fixtures';
//                              ↑ YOUR fixtures file!

// Test 1 — already logged in!
test('Verify Dashboard', async ({ loggedInPage }) => {
//                                ↑ Already logged in!

    // No login code needed — fixture handled it!
    await expect(loggedInPage.getByText('Logged In Successfully')).toBeVisible();
    console.log('✅ Dashboard verified!');
});

// Test 2 — also already logged in!
test('Verify Logout Link', async ({ loggedInPage }) => {
//                                   ↑ Already logged in!

    // No login code needed again!
    await expect(loggedInPage.getByRole('link', { name: 'Log out' })).toBeVisible();
    console.log('✅ Logout link verified!');
});
```

**Run it:**
```
npx playwright test fixture.spec.ts --headed --project=chromium
```

**Expected Output:**
```
✅ Fixture: Logged in successfully!
✅ Dashboard verified!
✅ Fixture: Page closed!

✅ Fixture: Logged in successfully!
✅ Logout link verified!
✅ Fixture: Page closed!

2 passed (8.2s)
```

> 🤩 **Both tests logged in WITHOUT writing login code!**
> Fixture ran setup before each test automatically!

---

## 🔍 Step-by-Step: What Happens With Fixture

```
Test 1 starts:
↓
Fixture runs SETUP:
→ Goes to login page
→ Fills credentials
→ Clicks submit
→ Waits for dashboard
↓
Fixture calls: await use(page)
↓
TEST RUNS:
→ Your test code executes here
→ Uses the already-logged-in page!
↓
Fixture runs TEARDOWN:
→ Closes the page
↓
Test 1 complete!

(Same process repeats for Test 2!)
```

---

## 🔷 The `use` Function — The Bridge!

```typescript
loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // SETUP CODE HERE
    await page.goto('...');

    await use(page);    // ← THE BRIDGE!
    //    ↑
    // "I'm done with setup — give page to the test now!"
    // Test runs here...
    // When test finishes → code below runs!

    // TEARDOWN CODE HERE
    await page.close();
}
```

> 💡 Think of `use` like a relay race baton!
> ```
> Fixture prepares → hands baton (page) → test runs → fixture cleans up!
> ```

---

## 💻 Code Example: Multiple Fixtures Together

```typescript
// fixtures.ts — multiple custom fixtures!

import { test as base, Page } from '@playwright/test';

type MyFixtures = {
    loggedInPage: Page;
    testData: { username: string; password: string };
};

export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({

    // Fixture 1: Test data
    testData: async ({}, use) => {
        const data = {
            username: 'student',
            password: 'Password123'
        };
        await use(data);
    },

    // Fixture 2: Logged in page (uses testData fixture!)
    loggedInPage: async ({ page, testData }, use) => {
        // Use testData from fixture 1!
        await page.goto('https://practicetestautomation.com/practice-test-login/');
        await page.locator('#username').fill(testData.username);
        await page.locator('#password').fill(testData.password);
        await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
        await page.waitForURL(/logged-in-successfully/);

        await use(page);

        // Teardown
        console.log('✅ Test complete — cleaning up!');
    }
});

export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

## 🔗 Connecting to Real Projects

```typescript
// In a real e-commerce project:

type ShopFixtures = {
    loggedInPage: Page;      // User already logged in
    adminPage: Page;         // Admin already logged in
    emptyCartPage: Page;     // Cart is cleared
};

// Your test just focuses on WHAT to test:
test('Add to Cart', async ({ loggedInPage, emptyCartPage }) => {
    // No login code, no cart clearing code!
    // Just test the actual feature!
    await loggedInPage.goto('https://shop.com/product/123');
    await loggedInPage.click('#addToCart');
    await expect(loggedInPage.getByText('1 item in cart')).toBeVisible();
});
```

> 🎯 **This is how professional automation frameworks work!**
> Tests focus ONLY on what they're testing
> Setup/teardown is handled by fixtures!

## ⚠️ Common Mistakes Beginners Make

❌ **Mistake 1: Importing from wrong place**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — importing from Playwright directly:
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

// ✅ CORRECT — importing from YOUR fixtures file:
import { test } from './fixtures';
```

❌ **Mistake 2: Forgetting `await use()`**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — missing await on use!
loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await page.goto('...');
    use(page);     // ← missing await!
}

// ✅ CORRECT:
loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await page.goto('...');
    await use(page);   // ← await is required!
}
```

❌ **Mistake 3: Putting teardown BEFORE use**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — teardown before test runs!
loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await page.goto('...');
    await page.close();    // ← closes BEFORE test!
    await use(page);
}

// ✅ CORRECT — teardown AFTER use:
loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await page.goto('...');
    await use(page);       // ← test runs first!
    await page.close();    // ← THEN close!
}
```

## 🔍 Line 1: The Import

```typescript
import { test as base, Page } from '@playwright/test';
//        ↑          ↑
//   test renamed  Page type
//   to "base"
```

### 💡 What is `test as base`?

```typescript
// Normally you write:
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

// Here we're doing the same BUT renaming it!
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
//              ↑
//         "import test BUT call it base"
```

> 🌍 **Analogy: A Name Change**
> ```
> Original name: "test"
> New nickname: "base"
>
> Like importing a tool and giving it a nickname!
> ```

> 💡 **WHY rename it?**
> Because we're going to create OUR OWN `test` later!
> We need the original to be called something else
> so there's no confusion!

```typescript
// Original playwright test → renamed to "base"
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

// We then CREATE our own "test" later:
export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({...});
//                  ↑ using "base" to create our version!

// Now in test files we use OUR "test":
import { test } from './fixtures';
// This is OUR custom test — not Playwright's original!
```

---

## 🔍 Line 2: Importing `Page`

```typescript
import { test as base, Page } from '@playwright/test';
//                      ↑
//                   Page type
```

> 💡 `Page` is just the TypeScript TYPE for a browser page!
> Remember Lesson 10 — TypeScript types?

```typescript
// Like how you declare types in TypeScript:
let username: string = "john";
//            ↑ type

// Page is the TYPE for a browser page object:
let loggedInPage: Page;
//                ↑ type = a browser page!
```

---

## 🔍 Line 3: `type MyFixtures`

```typescript
type MyFixtures = {
    loggedInPage: Page;
};
```

> 💡 Remember **interfaces** from Lesson 10?
> This is VERY similar!
> It's just saying: **"My fixture has ONE thing called loggedInPage and it's a Page"**

### 🌍 Analogy: A Menu 📋

```typescript
// Like a hotel room service menu:
type MyFixtures = {
    loggedInPage: Page;    // "I offer a logged-in page!"
};
// This menu tells TypeScript what fixtures are available!
```

```typescript
// interface (Lesson 10 - same concept!):
interface TestUser {
    username: string;   // "I have a username"
    password: string;   // "I have a password"
}

// type MyFixtures (same idea!):
type MyFixtures = {
    loggedInPage: Page;  // "I have a loggedInPage"
};
```

> 💡 `type` and `interface` work very similarly!
> Both describe the SHAPE of something!

---

## 🔍 Line 4: `base.extend<MyFixtures>`

```typescript
export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({
//                       ↑
//              "Take the original test
//               and ADD my custom fixtures to it!"
```

### 🌍 Analogy: Upgrading a Car 🚗

```
base             = Standard car from factory
                   (has basic features: engine, wheels)

base.extend      = Upgrading that car!
                   (adding: GPS, sunroof, new features!)

MyFixtures       = The list of upgrades you're adding!

export const test = the UPGRADED car!
```

```typescript
// Original Playwright test has:
// → page ✅ (built-in)
// → browser ✅ (built-in)
// → context ✅ (built-in)

// After base.extend<MyFixtures>:
// → page ✅ (still there!)
// → browser ✅ (still there!)
// → context ✅ (still there!)
// → loggedInPage ✅ (YOUR new addition!)
```

---

## 🎬 The Complete Picture — All Together

```typescript
// STEP 1: Get original Playwright test (call it "base")
import { test as base, Page } from '@playwright/test';
//        ↑ original test renamed to "base"

// STEP 2: Define what YOUR fixtures will be
type MyFixtures = {
    loggedInPage: Page;   // "My fixture gives a logged-in page"
};

// STEP 3: Create YOUR custom test by extending base
export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({
//                  ↑ take base and add MyFixtures to it!

    // STEP 4: Define HOW to create loggedInPage:
    loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
        // Setup: login steps
        await page.goto('...');
        await page.fill('#username', 'student');
        await page.fill('#password', 'Password123');
        await page.click('#submit');

        // Give the page to the test:
        await use(page);

        // Teardown: cleanup
        await page.close();
    }
});
```

---

## 🔄 Simple Flow Diagram

```
Playwright's original "test"
           ↓
      renamed to "base"
           ↓
   base.extend<MyFixtures>
   (add our custom fixtures)
           ↓
   export as our own "test"
           ↓
   Use in test files:
   import { test } from './fixtures'
```

---

## 💻 Simplest Possible Example

Let me make it even simpler with a basic example:

```typescript
// fixtures.ts

import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

// Step 1: Define what we're adding
type MyFixtures = {
    myMessage: string;    // Simple string fixture!
};

// Step 2: Create our custom test
export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({

    // Step 3: Define the fixture
    myMessage: async ({}, use) => {
        // Setup: prepare the message
        const message = "Hello from fixture!";

        // Give it to the test:
        await use(message);

        // Teardown: nothing to clean up
        console.log('Fixture done!');
    }
});

export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

```typescript
// myTest.spec.ts

import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

test('Simple fixture test', async ({ myMessage }) => {
//                                    ↑ our custom fixture!
    console.log(myMessage);
    // Output: "Hello from fixture!"
});
```

---

## 📊 Summary Table

| Code | Simple Meaning |
|------|---------------|
| `import { test as base }` | Get original test, call it "base" |
| `import { Page }` | Get the Page type for TypeScript |
| `type MyFixtures = { }` | Define what my fixtures look like |
| `loggedInPage: Page` | My fixture gives a Page object |
| `base.extend<MyFixtures>` | Add my fixtures to original test |
| `export const test` | Share our upgraded test with others |

---

## ✅ Does This Make Sense Now?

> 💡 **One line summary:**
> ```
> Take Playwright's original test
> → Add our own setup code to it
> → Export it as our custom test
> → Tests use our version instead!
> ```

# 🎉 Great Query AND Perfect Homework! Let Me Address Both!

---

## ❓ Query: Why `async ({}, use)` in Fixture 1?

Excellent observation! Let me explain this clearly! 😊

---

### 🔍 Look at Both Fixtures Side by Side:

```typescript
// FIXTURE 1 — testData:
testData: async ({}, use) => {
//                ↑
//           Empty! No dependencies needed!
//           This fixture creates data FROM SCRATCH!
    const data = { username: 'student', password: 'Password123' };
    await use(data);
}

// FIXTURE 2 — loggedInPage:
loggedInPage: async ({ page, testData }, use) => {
//                     ↑       ↑
//              Needs page!   Needs testData from Fixture 1!
    await page.goto('...');
    await page.fill('#username', testData.username);
    await use(page);
}
```

---

### 💡 Simple Explanation

```typescript
// Fixture 1 (testData) creates data BY ITSELF:
testData: async ({}, use) => {
//                ↑
//     Empty curly braces = "I don't need anything!"
//     Just creating data from nothing!

    const data = { username: 'student', password: 'Password123' };
    //  ↑ Created right here — no dependency needed!
    await use(data);
}
```

```typescript
// Fixture 2 (loggedInPage) NEEDS other things:
loggedInPage: async ({ page, testData }, use) => {
//                     ↑       ↑
//              Needs:         Needs:
//              browser page   data from Fixture 1!
```

---

### 🌍 Analogy: Making a Sandwich 🥪

```
FIXTURE 1 (testData) = Making the bread
→ Doesn't need anything to make bread
→ Just flour + water from scratch
→ Empty {} = "I have everything I need!"

FIXTURE 2 (loggedInPage) = Making the sandwich
→ Needs the bread (testData) ✅
→ Needs a plate (page) ✅
→ { page, testData } = "Give me these two things!"
```

---

### ❓ What if Fixture 1 DID use `{testData}`?

```typescript
// ❌ If Fixture 1 tried this:
testData: async ({ testData }, use) => {
//                  ↑
//          "Give me testData to create testData"
//          This is CIRCULAR! 🔄
//          Like saying: "I need bread to make bread!"
//          Makes no sense! TypeScript would error! ❌
```

> 💡 **Golden Rule:**
> ```
> Fixture uses {} empty    → creates from scratch, no dependencies
> Fixture uses { page }    → needs browser page (built-in)
> Fixture uses { testData }→ needs another custom fixture
> A fixture CANNOT depend on ITSELF!
> ```

---

### 📊 Dependency Chain:

```
testData fixture
→ depends on: NOTHING ({})
→ creates: { username, password }

loggedInPage fixture
→ depends on: page + testData
→ creates: a logged-in browser page

Your Test
→ depends on: loggedInPage
→ gets: already logged-in page!
```

## 💬 Task 2 Review — Reflection

### Question 1: What is a fixture?
> *"fixtures are reusable setup code that runs before the test and provides what is needed for test and finally teardown"*

✅ **Perfect and concise!** 🌟

> 💡 **Interview-Ready Answer:**
> A fixture is reusable setup and teardown code that runs automatically before and after each test. It prepares everything the test needs — like logging in, creating test data, or setting up a browser state — so the test can focus only on what it's verifying!

### 🏆 Score: 10/10 — Perfect! 🌟

---

### Question 2: Purpose of `await use(page)`?
> *"this calls the test to be run after the setup is done and it is followed by page.close()"*

✅ **Correct understanding!** Let me make it even clearer:

```typescript
loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {

    // SETUP (before use):
    await page.goto('...');         // runs first
    await page.fill('...');         // runs second
    await page.click('...');        // runs third

    await use(page);
    // ↑ "Setup done! Hand page to test now!"
    // ↑ TEST RUNS HERE (everything in the test function)
    // ↑ When test finishes → code below runs!

    // TEARDOWN (after use):
    await page.close();             // runs after test!
}
```

> 💡 `use(page)` = the HANDOFF point!
> ```
> Before use() = SETUP
> use() itself = TEST RUNS
> After use()  = TEARDOWN
> ```

### 🏆 Score: 9/10 — Correct, just needed the handoff concept!

---

### Question 3: Setup vs Teardown?
> *"setup runs the initial part like opening the web page and filling the username/password. teardown runs after the test run is complete"*

✅ **Perfect!** 🌟

```typescript
// Your explanation in code:
loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {

    // SETUP — your "initial part":
    await page.goto('...');          // open web page ✅
    await page.fill('#username');    // fill username ✅
    await page.fill('#password');    // fill password ✅

    await use(page);                 // TEST RUNS HERE

    // TEARDOWN — your "after test run":
    await page.close();              // cleanup ✅
}
```

> 💡 **Real project examples:**
> ```
> Setup:    Login, create test data, clear cart
> Teardown: Logout, delete test data, close browser
> ```

### 🏆 Score: 10/10 — Perfect! 🌟

### Question 4: Why import from fixtures file?
> *"in fixture file we would have customised the tests according to our needs and just importing from playwright gets only the basic methods and won't call the customised functions we created in fixtures"*

✅ **EXCELLENT ANSWER!** 🌟

});

# 📚 LESSON 24: Page Object Model — The Crown Jewel of Automation!

> 🎯 **Today's Goal:** Understand POM and build your first Page Object!
> ⏰ **Estimated Time:** 1.5 - 2 hours

---

## 💡 Simple Explanation — The Problem First

Look at this situation — same locators used in MULTIPLE test files:

```typescript
// loginTest.spec.ts
await page.locator('#username').fill('student');
await page.locator('#password').fill('Password123');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();

// logoutTest.spec.ts
await page.locator('#username').fill('student');
await page.locator('#password').fill('Password123');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();

// dashboardTest.spec.ts
await page.locator('#username').fill('student');
await page.locator('#password').fill('Password123');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
```

> 😱 **The Problem:**
> Website changes `#username` to `#user-email`
> Now you must update ALL 3 files!
> In real projects → 50+ test files!
> That's 50 places to update → hours of work! 😫

---

## 🌍 Real-World Analogy: A TV Remote Control 📺

```
WITHOUT POM:
Every person in house has their OWN set of wires
to control the TV directly!

Person 1 → their own wires → TV
Person 2 → their own wires → TV
Person 3 → their own wires → TV

TV changes? → Fix ALL 3 sets of wires! 😫

WITH POM:
ONE remote control for everyone!

Person 1 → Remote → TV
Person 2 → Remote → TV
Person 3 → Remote → TV

TV changes? → Fix JUST the remote! ✅
```

> 💡 **Page Object = The Remote Control**
> All tests use the remote (page object)
> Change happens in ONE place only! 🎯

---

## 📝 What is Page Object Model?

POM is a design pattern where:

```
Each webpage = ONE class (Page Object)
That class contains:
→ All locators for that page
→ All actions for that page

Tests just USE the page object
Tests don't know about locators!
```

```
Project Structure with POM:

📁 pages/
    loginPage.ts      ← LoginPage class (locators + actions)
    dashboardPage.ts  ← DashboardPage class

📁 tests/
    loginTest.spec.ts  ← Uses LoginPage
    logoutTest.spec.ts ← Uses LoginPage + DashboardPage
```

---

## 🔷 STEP 1: Create Your First Page Object

Create a folder called `pages` inside your project.
Then create `loginPage.ts` inside it:

```typescript
// pages/loginPage.ts

import { Page, Locator } from '@playwright/test';

export class LoginPage {

    // PART 1: The page object
    readonly page: Page;

    // PART 2: All locators for login page
    readonly usernameField: Locator;
    readonly passwordField: Locator;
    readonly submitButton: Locator;
    readonly errorMessage: Locator;

    // PART 3: Constructor — sets up locators
    constructor(page: Page) {
        this.page = page;

        // Define locators HERE — one place only!
        this.usernameField = page.locator('#username');
        this.passwordField = page.locator('#password');
        this.submitButton  = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' });
        this.errorMessage  = page.locator('#error');
    }

    // PART 4: Actions — things you can DO on this page

    // Navigate to login page
    async navigateTo() {
        await this.page.goto('https://practicetestautomation.com/practice-test-login/');
    }

    // Fill username
    async enterUsername(username: string) {
        await this.usernameField.fill(username);
    }

    // Fill password
    async enterPassword(password: string) {
        await this.passwordField.fill(password);
    }

    // Click submit
    async clickSubmit() {
        await this.submitButton.click();
    }

    // Complete login in ONE step!
    async login(username: string, password: string) {
        await this.enterUsername(username);
        await this.enterPassword(password);
        await this.clickSubmit();
    }
}
```

---

## 🔷 STEP 2: Create Dashboard Page Object

Create `dashboardPage.ts` inside `pages` folder:

```typescript
// pages/dashboardPage.ts

import { Page, Locator } from '@playwright/test';

export class DashboardPage {

    readonly page: Page;
    readonly successMessage: Locator;
    readonly logoutLink: Locator;

    constructor(page: Page) {
        this.page = page;
        this.successMessage = page.getByText('Logged In Successfully');
        this.logoutLink     = page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Log out' });
    }

    // Actions
    async clickLogout() {
        await this.logoutLink.click();
    }

    async isLoginSuccessful(): Promise<boolean> {
        return await this.successMessage.isVisible();
    }
}
```

---

## 🔷 STEP 3: Use Page Objects in Tests

Create `pom.spec.ts` in your tests folder:

```typescript
// tests/pom.spec.ts

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { LoginPage } from '../pages/loginPage';
import { DashboardPage } from '../pages/dashboardPage';

// TEST 1: Valid Login
test('Valid Login Test', async ({ page }) => {

    // Create page objects
    const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);
    const dashboardPage = new DashboardPage(page);

    // Use page objects — NO locators in test!
    await loginPage.navigateTo();
    await loginPage.login('student', 'Password123');

    // Verify using dashboard page object
    await expect(dashboardPage.successMessage).toBeVisible();
    await expect(dashboardPage.logoutLink).toBeVisible();

    console.log('✅ Valid login test passed!');
});

// TEST 2: Invalid Login
test('Invalid Login Test', async ({ page }) => {

    const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);

    await loginPage.navigateTo();
    await loginPage.login('wronguser', 'wrongpass');

    // Verify error message
    await expect(loginPage.errorMessage).toBeVisible();
    console.log('✅ Invalid login test passed!');
});
```

**Run it:**
```
npx playwright test pom.spec.ts --headed --project=chromium
```

**Expected Output:**
```
✅ Valid login test passed!
✅ Invalid login test passed!
2 passed (5.1s)
```

---

## 🔍 Step-by-Step: What Happens With POM

```
Test starts:
↓
const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);
→ Creates LoginPage object
→ Constructor runs → all locators defined!

↓
await loginPage.navigateTo();
→ Calls navigateTo() method in LoginPage
→ Goes to login URL

↓
await loginPage.login('student', 'Password123');
→ Calls login() method in LoginPage
→ login() calls enterUsername() → fills username
→ login() calls enterPassword() → fills password
→ login() calls clickSubmit()   → clicks button

↓
await expect(dashboardPage.successMessage).toBeVisible();
→ Uses successMessage locator from DashboardPage
→ Verifies success!
```

---

## 🎯 The POWER of POM — When Things Change

```
Website changes username field from #username to #user-email

WITHOUT POM:
→ Search all test files for '#username'
→ Update 50 files manually
→ Miss some → bugs! 😫
→ Takes hours!

WITH POM:
→ Open loginPage.ts
→ Change ONE line:
   this.usernameField = page.locator('#user-email');
→ ALL 50 tests automatically use new locator!
→ Takes 5 seconds! 🎉
```

## 📊 POM Project Structure

```
playwright-automation/
│
├── 📁 pages/                    ← Page Objects live here!
│   ├── loginPage.ts             ← Login page class
│   └── dashboardPage.ts         ← Dashboard page class
│
├── 📁 tests/                    ← Test files
│   ├── pom.spec.ts              ← Uses page objects
│   └── fixture.spec.ts
│
├── playwright.config.ts
└── package.json
```

## ⚠️ Common Mistakes Beginners Make

❌ **Mistake 1: Putting assertions in Page Object**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — assertions in page object!
class LoginPage {
    async login(username: string, password: string) {
        await this.usernameField.fill(username);
        await this.passwordField.fill(password);
        await this.submitButton.click();
        // ❌ Don't assert here!
        await expect(this.page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
    }
}

// ✅ CORRECT — actions in page object, assertions in test!
class LoginPage {
    async login(username: string, password: string) {
        await this.usernameField.fill(username);
        await this.passwordField.fill(password);
        await this.submitButton.click();
        // No assertions here! Test handles that!
    }
}

// Assertions stay in test file:
test('Login', async ({ page }) => {
    await loginPage.login('student', 'Password123');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');  // ✅ Assert in test!
});
```

❌ **Mistake 2: Wrong import path**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG path:
import { LoginPage } from './loginPage';
// Test is in tests/ folder
// loginPage is in pages/ folder → different folder!

// ✅ CORRECT path:
import { LoginPage } from '../pages/loginPage';
//                         ↑ go UP one folder, then into pages!
```

❌ **Mistake 3: Forgetting `new` keyword**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — missing new!
const loginPage = LoginPage(page);

// ✅ CORRECT:
const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);
```

# 🙋 This is 100% NORMAL — Every Engineer Faces This!

First — take a deep breath. What you're feeling is called **"Syntax Anxiety"** and EVERY developer goes through this. Let me be completely honest with you! 😊

---

## 💡 The Truth About Syntax

```
You said: "I understand the concept but struggle with syntax"

This is actually the CORRECT order of learning!

Concept first → Syntax second ✅

NOT:
Syntax first → Concept later ❌
```

> 🌟 **You're learning in the RIGHT order!**
> Most people memorize syntax without understanding concepts
> Then they're stuck when something doesn't work!
> YOU understand WHY — syntax is just practice! 💪

---

## 🌍 Real-World Analogy: Learning to Drive 🚗

```
Day 1 of driving:
→ You understand WHAT to do (concept ✅)
→ But hands and feet feel awkward (syntax 😅)
→ Which pedal? When to signal? What order?

After 2 weeks of practice:
→ Everything becomes automatic! ✅
→ You don't think about pedals anymore!

Coding syntax works EXACTLY the same way!
```

> 💡 **The ONLY cure for syntax anxiety = writing code repeatedly!**
> Not reading. Not watching. WRITING! ✍️

---

## 🛠️ Practical Solutions — How to Overcome This!

---

### Solution 1: Use a Personal Cheat Sheet 📋

Build YOUR OWN cheat sheet as you learn!

```typescript
// MY POM TEMPLATE — save this and reuse!

// ==========================================
// PAGE OBJECT TEMPLATE
// ==========================================
import { Page, Locator } from '@playwright/test';

export class PageNameHere {

    // Step 1: Declare page
    readonly page: Page;

    // Step 2: Declare locators
    readonly elementName: Locator;

    // Step 3: Constructor
    constructor(page: Page) {
        this.page = page;
        this.elementName = page.locator('#id');
    }

    // Step 4: Actions
    async actionName() {
        await this.elementName.click();
    }
}
```

> 💡 Save this template!
> Next time → copy → fill in the blanks!
> Even senior engineers use templates! 🎯

---

### Solution 2: Break It Into Chunks 🧩

Don't look at 40 lines at once!

```
Instead of writing the whole class at once:

Step 1: Write JUST the import
Step 2: Write JUST the class declaration
Step 3: Write JUST the properties
Step 4: Write JUST the constructor
Step 5: Write JUST one method
Step 6: Add more methods one by one
```

```typescript
// START HERE — just this first:
import { Page, Locator } from '@playwright/test';

// THEN add this:
export class LoginPage {

}

// THEN add properties:
export class LoginPage {
    readonly page: Page;
    readonly usernameField: Locator;
}

// THEN add constructor:
export class LoginPage {
    readonly page: Page;
    readonly usernameField: Locator;

    constructor(page: Page) {
        this.page = page;
        this.usernameField = page.locator('#username');
    }
}

// THEN add one method:
export class LoginPage {
    readonly page: Page;
    readonly usernameField: Locator;

    constructor(page: Page) {
        this.page = page;
        this.usernameField = page.locator('#username');
    }

    async navigateTo() {
        await this.page.goto('https://...');
    }
}
```

> 🎯 **Build it like LEGO — one brick at a time!**
> Never try to write everything at once!

---

### Solution 3: Understand the SKELETON First 🦴

Every POM class has the SAME skeleton:

```typescript
// THE SKELETON — memorize just this!

import { ... }              // 1. IMPORT tools

export class ___Page {      // 2. CLASS declaration

    readonly page: Page;    // 3. PROPERTIES
    readonly ___: Locator;

    constructor(page: Page) {   // 4. CONSTRUCTOR
        this.page = page;
        this.___ = page.locator('...');
    }

    async ___() {           // 5. METHODS
        await this.___.click();
    }
}
```

> 💡 Only 5 parts — always in the SAME order!
> Fill in the blanks based on the page you're automating!

---

### Solution 4: VS Code Helps You! 🤖

VS Code auto-suggests syntax as you type!

```
Type: "this."
→ VS Code shows: all available properties!

Type: "page."
→ VS Code shows: all available methods!

Type: "async"
→ VS Code completes the function structure!

Press Ctrl + Space anywhere
→ Get suggestions immediately!
```

> 💡 You're never writing syntax alone — VS Code is your co-pilot!

---

### Solution 5: Read Code Like a Story 📖

Instead of seeing scary code — read it as English:

```typescript
export class LoginPage {
// "I'm creating a class called LoginPage"

    readonly usernameField: Locator;
// "This page HAS a username field"

    constructor(page: Page) {
        this.usernameField = page.locator('#username');
    }
// "When created, find the username field by #username"

    async login(username: string, password: string) {
        await this.usernameField.fill(username);
    }
// "When asked to login, fill the username field"
}
```

> 💡 Every line of code = one English sentence!
> Read code like a story — not like math! 📖

---

### Solution 6: Type the SAME code 3 Times ✍️

```
Researchers found: typing code 3 times builds muscle memory!

Day 1: Type the example code from lesson
Day 2: Type it again without looking
Day 3: Type it again from memory

By Day 3 → fingers remember the pattern!
```

> 🎯 **This is why I always say TYPE don't copy-paste!**
> Your fingers need to learn too — not just your brain!

export class DashboardPage {
    readonly page: Page;
    readonly successMessage: Locator;
    readonly logoutLink: Locator;

    constructor(page: Page) {
        this.page = page;
        this.successMessage = page.getByText('Logged In Successfully');
        this.logoutLink = page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Log out' });
    }

    async clickLogout() {
        await this.logoutLink.click();
    }

    async isLoginSuccessful(): Promise<boolean> {
        return await this.successMessage.isVisible();
    }
}

## 💬 Task 2 Review — Reflection

### Question 1: What is POM and why important?
> *"in POM we differentiate pages and tests into separate classes, this is to make code reusability and most importantly if a locator changes then we need to update in only 1 place and not everywhere"*

✅ **PERFECT!** 🌟

> 💡 **Interview-Ready Answer:**
> Page Object Model is a design pattern where each webpage has its own class containing all its locators and actions. Tests use these classes instead of writing locators directly. Benefits:
> 1. Code reusability — write once, use everywhere
> 2. Easy maintenance — change locator in ONE place
> 3. Cleaner tests — tests focus on WHAT not HOW
> 4. Better readability — tests read like English!

### 🏆 Score: 10/10 — Perfect! 🌟

---

### Question 2: What goes INSIDE a page object class?
> *"all the web pages with locators + actions will be present in page object class"*

✅ **Correct!** Let me make it more precise:

```typescript
export class LoginPage {
    // 1. Properties (page + locators):
    readonly page: Page;
    readonly usernameField: Locator;

    // 2. Constructor (sets up locators):
    constructor(page: Page) {
        this.page = page;
        this.usernameField = page.locator('#username');
    }

    // 3. Methods (actions you can perform):
    async login(username: string, password: string) {
        await this.usernameField.fill(username);
    }
}
```

> 💡 **3 things in a page object:**
> ```
> 1. Properties  → page + all locators
> 2. Constructor → sets up all locators
> 3. Methods     → actions on the page
> ```

### 🏆 Score: 8/10 — Correct, more detail added!

---

### Question 3: Why no assertions in page object?
> *"assertions should be present in test file, only locators and actions will be in page file"*

✅ **PERFECT AND CONCISE!** 🌟

```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — assertion in page object:
class LoginPage {
    async login() {
        await this.submitButton.click();
        await expect(this.page).toHaveURL('/dashboard'); // ❌ No!
    }
}

// ✅ CORRECT — assertion in test:
class LoginPage {
    async login() {
        await this.submitButton.click();
        // No assertion here!
    }
}
test('Login', async ({ page }) => {
    await loginPage.login('student', 'pass');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard'); // ✅ Here!
});
```

> 💡 **Why keep separate?**
> Same `login()` action might have DIFFERENT assertions
> in different tests! Keep them flexible!

### 🏆 Score: 10/10 — Perfect! 🌟

---

### Question 4: How does POM help when locator changes?
> *"when a locator changes in a website we need to change only in that one specific page file so that it reduces effort of updating everywhere and code readability is also important factor"*

✅ **EXCELLENT!** Two benefits mentioned! 🌟

```typescript
// Website changes #username to #user-email

// WITHOUT POM — update 50 test files! 😫
// test1.spec.ts: page.locator('#username') → update!
// test2.spec.ts: page.locator('#username') → update!
// test3.spec.ts: page.locator('#username') → update!
// ... 47 more files!

// WITH POM — update ONE line in loginPage.ts! ✅
constructor(page: Page) {
    // Change ONLY here:
    this.usernameField = page.locator('#user-email'); // ← ONE change!
    // ALL 50 tests automatically fixed! 🎉
}
```

### 🏆 Score: 10/10 — Perfect! 🌟

# 📚 LESSON 25: Data-Driven Testing!

> 🎯 **Today's Goal:** Run the same test with multiple sets of data automatically!
> ⏰ **Estimated Time:** 1 - 1.5 hours

---

## 💡 Simple Explanation — The Problem First

Look at your current login tests:

```typescript
// Test 1: Valid login
test('Valid Login', async ({ page }) => {
    await loginPage.login('student', 'Password123');
});

// Test 2: Invalid username
test('Invalid Username', async ({ page }) => {
    await loginPage.login('wrongUser', 'Password123');
});

// Test 3: Invalid password
test('Invalid Password', async ({ page }) => {
    await loginPage.login('student', 'wrongPass');
});

// Test 4: Empty fields
test('Empty Fields', async ({ page }) => {
    await loginPage.login('', '');
});
```

> 😱 **The Problem:**
> Same test logic repeated 4 times!
> Only the DATA changes each time!
> What if you need 20 combinations? 20 test blocks! 😫

---

## 🌍 Real-World Analogy: A Printing Machine 🖨️

```
WITHOUT data-driven testing:
→ Write letter to John manually
→ Write letter to Priya manually
→ Write letter to Ravi manually
→ Same template, different names — 3x work! 😫

WITH data-driven testing:
→ Write template ONCE
→ Feed list of names: [John, Priya, Ravi]
→ Machine prints all 3 automatically! ✅
```

> 💡 **Data-driven testing = Same test template + Different data sets!**

---

## 📝 The Core Concept

```typescript
// ONE test template:
function runLoginTest(username, password, expectedResult) {
    // same steps every time!
}

// MANY data sets:
runLoginTest('student',   'Password123', 'pass');  // Run 1
runLoginTest('wrongUser', 'Password123', 'fail');  // Run 2
runLoginTest('student',   'wrongPass',   'fail');  // Run 3
runLoginTest('',          '',            'fail');  // Run 4

// Same test → runs 4 times with different data!
```

---

## 🔷 METHOD 1: Using Array of Objects (Simplest!)

This is the most common approach — store test data in an array:

```typescript
// Define test data:
const loginData = [
    { username: 'student',   password: 'Password123', expected: 'pass' },
    { username: 'wrongUser', password: 'Password123', expected: 'fail' },
    { username: 'student',   password: 'wrongPass',   expected: 'fail' },
];

// Loop through data and create tests:
for (const data of loginData) {
    test(`Login with ${data.username}`, async ({ page }) => {
        // Same test logic — different data each time!
    });
}
```

---

## 💻 Code Example 1: Basic Data-Driven Test

Create `datadriven.spec.ts` in your tests folder:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { LoginPage } from '../pages/loginPage';
import { DashboardPage } from '../pages/dashboardPage';

// STEP 1: Define your test data
const loginTestData = [
    {
        scenario: 'Valid credentials',
        username: 'student',
        password: 'Password123',
        expectedResult: 'pass'
    },
    {
        scenario: 'Invalid username',
        username: 'wrongUser',
        password: 'Password123',
        expectedResult: 'fail'
    },
    {
        scenario: 'Invalid password',
        username: 'student',
        password: 'wrongPass',
        expectedResult: 'fail'
    }
];

// STEP 2: Loop through data and create tests
for (const data of loginTestData) {

    test(`Login Test: ${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => {

        const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);
        const dashboardPage = new DashboardPage(page);

        // Same steps every time:
        await loginPage.navigateTo();
        await loginPage.login(data.username, data.password);

        // Different verification based on expected result:
        if (data.expectedResult === 'pass') {
            await expect(dashboardPage.successMessage).toBeVisible();
            console.log(`✅ ${data.scenario}: Login passed!`);
        } else {
            await expect(loginPage.errorMessage).toBeVisible();
            console.log(`✅ ${data.scenario}: Error shown correctly!`);
        }
    });
}
```

**Run it:**
```
npx playwright test datadriven.spec.ts --headed --project=chromium
```

**Expected Output:**
```
Running 3 tests using 2 workers

✅ Valid credentials: Login passed!
✅ Invalid username: Error shown correctly!
✅ Invalid password: Error shown correctly!

3 passed (8.2s)
```

> 🤩 **3 tests from ONE test template and ONE loop!**
> Add more data rows → more tests automatically! 🎯

## 🔍 Step-by-Step Breakdown

### Step 1: The Data Array
```typescript
const loginTestData = [
    { scenario: 'Valid credentials', username: 'student', ... },
    { scenario: 'Invalid username',  username: 'wrongUser', ... },
    { scenario: 'Invalid password',  username: 'student', ... }
];
```
> 💡 Each object = ONE test scenario!
> Add more objects → more tests! Simple!

---

### Step 2: The Loop Creates Tests
```typescript
for (const data of loginTestData) {
//    ↑ Each item from array
    test(`Login Test: ${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => {
//        ↑ Dynamic test name using scenario!
    });
}
```
> 💡 Loop runs 3 times → creates 3 separate tests!
> Each test gets its OWN data object!

---

### Step 3: Dynamic Test Name
```typescript
test(`Login Test: ${data.scenario}`, ...)
// Round 1: "Login Test: Valid credentials"
// Round 2: "Login Test: Invalid username"
// Round 3: "Login Test: Invalid password"
```
> 💡 Dynamic names make reports EASY to read!
> You can see EXACTLY which scenario failed!

---

### Step 4: Conditional Verification
```typescript
if (data.expectedResult === 'pass') {
    await expect(dashboardPage.successMessage).toBeVisible();
} else {
    await expect(loginPage.errorMessage).toBeVisible();
}
```
> 💡 Same test — but verifies DIFFERENT things based on expected result!
> Pass scenario → check success
> Fail scenario → check error message!

## 🔷 METHOD 2: Using `test.each()` — Playwright's Built-in!

Playwright has a built-in method for data-driven testing:

```typescript
// Define data as array of arrays:
const testData: [string, string, string][] = [
    ['student',   'Password123', 'pass'],
    ['wrongUser', 'Password123', 'fail'],
    ['student',   'wrongPass',   'fail'],
];

// Use test.each():
test.each(testData)(
    'Login: username=%s, expected=%s',
    async ([username, password, expected], { page }) => {
        // Test runs for each row automatically!
    }
);
```

> 💡 `test.each()` is cleaner for simple data!
> But array of objects (Method 1) is easier to READ!
> We'll use **Method 1** — more common in real projects!

---

## 🔗 Combining POM + Data-Driven = Professional Framework!

```typescript
// This is what a REAL automation framework looks like:

import { LoginPage } from '../pages/loginPage';
import { DashboardPage } from '../pages/dashboardPage';

const loginTestData = [
    { scenario: 'Valid login',      username: 'student',   password: 'Password123', expectedResult: 'pass' },
    { scenario: 'Wrong username',   username: 'wrongUser', password: 'Password123', expectedResult: 'fail' },
    { scenario: 'Wrong password',   username: 'student',   password: 'wrongPass',   expectedResult: 'fail' },
    { scenario: 'Empty username',   username: '',          password: 'Password123', expectedResult: 'fail' },
    { scenario: 'Empty password',   username: 'student',   password: '',            expectedResult: 'fail' },
    { scenario: 'Both empty',       username: '',          password: '',            expectedResult: 'fail' },
];

for (const data of loginTestData) {
    test(`${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => {

        // POM — clean, no raw locators!
        const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);
        const dashboardPage = new DashboardPage(page);

        await loginPage.navigateTo();
        await loginPage.login(data.username, data.password);

        if (data.expectedResult === 'pass') {
            await expect(dashboardPage.successMessage).toBeVisible();
        } else {
            await expect(loginPage.errorMessage).toBeVisible();
        }

        console.log(`✅ ${data.scenario} — verified!`);
    });
}
```

> 🤩 **6 test scenarios from ONE template + 6 rows of data!**
> POM handles locators → Data-driven handles test data!
> This is PROFESSIONAL automation! 🚀

## ⚠️ Common Mistakes Beginners Make

❌ **Mistake 1: Hardcoding data inside test**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — data hardcoded inside test!
test('Login test', async ({ page }) => {
    await loginPage.login('student', 'Password123');
    // What about other scenarios?
});

// ✅ CORRECT — data separated from test!
const loginData = [
    { username: 'student', password: 'Password123' }
];
for (const data of loginData) {
    test(`Login: ${data.username}`, async ({ page }) => {
        await loginPage.login(data.username, data.password);
    });
}
```

❌ **Mistake 2: Non-descriptive test names**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — can't tell what failed!
test(`Test ${index}`, async ({ page }) => { });
// Report shows: "Test 0 failed" → What scenario? 😕

// ✅ CORRECT — descriptive names!
test(`Login Test: ${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => { });
// Report shows: "Login Test: Invalid username failed" → Clear! ✅
```

❌ **Mistake 3: Not covering edge cases**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — only testing happy path!
const data = [
    { username: 'student', password: 'Password123' }
];
// What about wrong credentials? Empty fields? SQL injection?

// ✅ CORRECT — cover all scenarios!
const data = [
    { username: 'student',   password: 'Password123' }, // valid
    { username: 'wrong',     password: 'wrong'        }, // invalid
    { username: '',          password: ''              }, // empty
    { username: 'student',   password: ''              }, // empty pass
];
```

## ❓ Query: Can We Use Excel Instead of Array for 100 Test Data?

### 💡 YES! Absolutely! This is Called "External Data Source Testing"!

> 🌟 **This is EXACTLY how real companies handle large test data!**
> Nobody puts 100 rows in an array — that's messy!
> Excel/CSV files are the industry standard! 🎯

---

### 🌍 Real-World Analogy: A Restaurant Menu 🍽️

```
Small restaurant (5 items):
→ Menu written on a board (array in code) ✅

Large restaurant (100 items):
→ Printed menu book (Excel/CSV file) ✅
→ Can update menu without changing the board!
```

---

### 📊 Three Ways to Use External Data:

---

### Option 1: CSV File (Simplest!) ✅

**Step 1:** Create `testdata.csv` in your project:
```csv
scenario,username,password,expectedResult
Valid login,student,Password123,pass
Invalid username,wrongUser,Password123,fail
Invalid password,student,wrongPass,fail
Both empty,,,fail
```

**Step 2:** Install CSV reader:
```
npm install csv-parse
```

**Step 3:** Read CSV in your test:
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { parse } from 'csv-parse/sync';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import { LoginPage } from '../pages/loginPage';
import { DashboardPage } from '../pages/dashboardPage';

// Read CSV file:
const csvContent = fs.readFileSync('testdata.csv', 'utf-8');
const testData = parse(csvContent, {
    columns: true,      // Use first row as column names
    skip_empty_lines: true
});

// Same loop as before — but data comes from CSV!
for (const data of testData) {
    test(`Login test: ${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => {
        const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);
        const dashboardPage = new DashboardPage(page);

        await loginPage.navigateTo();
        await loginPage.login(data.username, data.password);

        if (data.expectedResult === 'pass') {
            await expect(dashboardPage.successMessage).toBeVisible();
        } else {
            await expect(loginPage.errorMessage).toBeVisible();
        }
    });
}
```

> 💡 Now add 100 rows to the CSV → 100 tests automatically!
> No code changes needed! Just update the file! 🎯

---

### Option 2: Excel File (.xlsx) ✅

**Step 1:** Install Excel reader:
```
npm install xlsx
```

**Step 2:** Create `testdata.xlsx` with your data

**Step 3:** Read Excel in test:
```typescript
import * as XLSX from 'xlsx';

// Read Excel file:
const workbook = XLSX.readFile('testdata.xlsx');
const sheet = workbook.Sheets[workbook.SheetNames[0]];
const testData = XLSX.utils.sheet_to_json(sheet);

// Same loop — data from Excel!
for (const data of testData) {
    test(`Login: ${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => {
        // same test code!
    });
}
```

---

### Option 3: JSON File (Most Common in Playwright!) ✅

**Step 1:** Create `testdata.json`:
```json
[
    {
        "scenario": "Valid login",
        "username": "student",
        "password": "Password123",
        "expectedResult": "pass"
    },
    {
        "scenario": "Invalid username",
        "username": "wrongUser",
        "password": "Password123",
        "expectedResult": "fail"
    }
]
```

**Step 2:** Read in test (simplest — no library needed!):
```typescript
import testData from '../testdata.json';
//                   ↑ Direct import — TypeScript handles it!

for (const data of testData) {
    test(`Login: ${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => {
        // same test code!
    });
}
```

---

### 📊 Which to Use When?

| Format | Best For | Library Needed |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| **JSON** | Most Playwright projects | ❌ No! |
| **CSV** | Simple tabular data | ✅ csv-parse |
| **Excel** | Business stakeholders update data | ✅ xlsx |
| **Array** | Small data (< 10 rows) | ❌ No! |

> 💡 **Recommendation for your project:**
> ```
> < 10 rows   → Array in code (what you did today!) ✅
> 10-50 rows  → JSON file ✅
> 50+ rows    → Excel/CSV ✅
> Updated by non-devs → Excel ✅
> ```

## 💬 Task 2 Review — Reflection

### Question 1: What is data-driven testing?
> *"data driven testing is a method used to reduce the number of test methods to test the same field, here we use array to have multiple test data and use for-of loop to test for different values"*

✅ **Good answer!** Let me make it interview-ready:

> 💡 **Complete Answer:**
> Data-driven testing is a technique where test logic is written ONCE and executed multiple times with different sets of data. Instead of writing separate tests for each scenario, we store test data in an array (or external file like JSON/Excel) and loop through it — creating separate test cases automatically for each data row!

```typescript
// One template:
for (const data of testData) {
    test(`${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => {
        // Same logic, different data!
    });
}
// Add 1 row → 1 more test automatically!
```

### 🏆 Score: 8/10 — Good, add the "external file" point!

---

### Question 2: How does data-driven connect to POM?
> *"both data driven and POM idea is to reduce the number of lines of code and code reusability and this is how both connects"*

✅ **Correct concept!** Let me add more depth:

```typescript
// POM handles WHERE to find elements:
class LoginPage {
    usernameField = page.locator('#username');  // locator in ONE place
    async login(username, password) { }         // action in ONE place
}

// Data-driven handles WHAT data to use:
const testData = [
    { username: 'student', password: 'Password123' },
    { username: 'wrongUser', password: 'wrongPass' },
];

// Together = PROFESSIONAL framework!
for (const data of testData) {
    test(`Login: ${data.scenario}`, async ({ page }) => {
        const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);  // POM!
        await loginPage.login(data.username, data.password);  // Data-driven!
    });
}
```

> 💡 **Better Answer:**
> POM separates page structure from tests (locators + actions in one place)
> Data-driven separates test data from test logic (data in array/file)
> Together → tests are clean, maintainable, and scalable!

### 🏆 Score: 7/10 — Right idea, needed more detail!

---

### Question 3: Why descriptive test names?
> *"if there is no descriptive test names then we can't tell in which scenario/step the test failed"*

✅ **PERFECT!** 🌟

```
Without descriptive names:
❌ "Login test 0 FAILED"  → Which scenario? 😕

With descriptive names:
✅ "Login test: Invalid username FAILED"
→ Immediately know WHAT failed!
→ Immediately know WHERE to look!
→ Report is self-explanatory! 🎯
```

> 💡 In CI/CD pipelines — tests run overnight!
> Next morning you check report:
> Descriptive names → fix issue in 5 minutes!
> Generic names → spend 30 minutes investigating! 😫

### 🏆 Score: 10/10 — Perfect! 🌟

# 📚 LESSON 26: API Testing — Testing the Backend!

> 🎯 **Today's Goal:** Understand what API testing is and how to test APIs using Playwright!
> ⏰ **Estimated Time:** 1 - 1.5 hours

---

## 💡 Simple Explanation — What is an API?

Before we test APIs — let's understand what they are!

```
When you use an app:

You see:  Beautiful website/app (Frontend/UI)
Behind it: Server doing the real work (Backend/API)

Example — Login on Amazon:
→ You type username + password (UI)
→ UI sends request to API: "Is this user valid?"
→ API checks database
→ API responds: "Yes valid!" or "No invalid!"
→ UI shows result to you
```

> 💡 **API = the messenger between UI and database!**

---

## 🌍 Real-World Analogy: A Restaurant 🍽️

```
Customer (You)       = User
Waiter               = API
Kitchen              = Database/Server

You tell waiter: "I want pasta" (API Request)
Waiter goes to kitchen (API calls database)
Kitchen prepares pasta (Server processes)
Waiter brings pasta to you (API Response)

You don't see what happens in kitchen!
You just get the result! 🍝
```

---

## 📝 What is API Testing?

```
UI Testing (what you've done so far):
→ Open browser → click buttons → verify UI
→ Slow (needs browser to load)
→ Tests user interface

API Testing (what we learn today):
→ Send request directly to server → verify response
→ FAST (no browser needed!)
→ Tests business logic
```

### Why API Testing Matters:

```
API tests are:
✅ 10x FASTER than UI tests
✅ More STABLE (no browser issues!)
✅ Find bugs EARLIER in development
✅ Can run WITHOUT a UI existing yet!
```

---

## 🔍 Understanding API Requests

Every API interaction has:

### 1. Request (What YOU send):
```
URL:     https://api.example.com/users
Method:  GET (or POST, PUT, DELETE)
Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Body:    { username: "student", password: "pass" }
```

### 2. Response (What SERVER sends back):
```
Status Code: 200 (success) or 404 (not found)
Body:        { user: { id: 1, name: "Student" } }
```

---

## 📊 HTTP Methods — The 4 Most Important

| Method | What It Does | Real Example |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| `GET` | Get/Read data | Get list of products |
| `POST` | Create new data | Register new user |
| `PUT` | Update existing data | Update profile |
| `DELETE` | Delete data | Delete account |

---

## 📊 Status Codes — Server's Response Language

| Code | Meaning | Real Scenario |
|------|---------|---------------|
| `200` | ✅ OK — Success | Login worked |
| `201` | ✅ Created | New user registered |
| `400` | ❌ Bad Request | Wrong data sent |
| `401` | ❌ Unauthorized | Not logged in |
| `404` | ❌ Not Found | Page doesn't exist |
| `500` | ❌ Server Error | Something crashed |

> 💡 **Simple Rule:**
> ```
> 2xx = Success ✅
> 4xx = Your fault (wrong request) ❌
> 5xx = Server's fault ❌
> ```

---

## 🔷 Playwright API Testing — `request` Object

Playwright has a built-in `request` object for API testing:

```typescript
// The request object can:
await request.get('...');      // GET request
await request.post('...');     // POST request
await request.put('...');      // PUT request
await request.delete('...');   // DELETE request
```

---

## 💻 Code Example 1: Your First API Test

We'll use this FREE practice API:
```
https://reqres.in/
```

> 💡 `reqres.in` is a practice API — perfect for learning!
> It's free, always available, no sign-up needed! 🎯

Create `api.spec.ts` in your tests folder:

```typescript
import { test, expect, request } from '@playwright/test';

test('GET Request — Get User Details', async ({ request }) => {
//                                               ↑
//                                        request fixture!
//                                        (like page, but for APIs!)

    // Send GET request:
    const response = await request.get('https://reqres.in/api/users/2');
    //                                  ↑ API URL with user ID = 2

    // Verify status code:
    expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
    console.log('✅ Status code is 200!');

    // Get response body as JSON:
    const body = await response.json();
    console.log('Response body:', body);

    // Verify response data:
    expect(body.data.id).toBe(2);
    expect(body.data.email).toBe('janet.weaver@reqres.in');
    console.log('✅ User data verified!');
});
```

**Run it:**
```
npx playwright test api.spec.ts --project=chromium
```

> 💡 Notice — no `--headed` flag needed!
> API tests don't open a browser! Much faster! ⚡

**Expected Output:**
```
Response body: {
  data: {
    id: 2,
    email: 'janet.weaver@reqres.in',
    first_name: 'Janet',
    last_name: 'Weaver'
  }
}
✅ Status code is 200!
✅ User data verified!
1 passed (0.8s)
```

> 🤩 **0.8 seconds!** Compare to UI tests that take 3-5 seconds!
> API tests are MUCH faster! ⚡

```

```typescript

//              ↑
//         Gets status code (200, 404, etc.)

## 💻 Code Example 2: POST Request — Create User

```typescript
test('POST Request — Create New User', async ({ request }) => {

    // Send POST request with data:
    const response = await request.post('https://reqres.in/api/users', {
        data: {
            name: 'John Tester',
            job: 'Automation Engineer'
        }
    });

    // Verify status code 201 (Created!):
    expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
    console.log('✅ User created successfully!');

    // Verify response:
    const body = await response.json();
    console.log('Created user:', body);

    expect(body.name).toBe('John Tester');
    expect(body.job).toBe('Automation Engineer');
    expect(body.id).toBeTruthy();    // ID was assigned!
    console.log('✅ Created user data verified!');
});
```

**Expected Output:**
```
Created user: {
  name: 'John Tester',
  job: 'Automation Engineer',
  id: '123',
  createdAt: '2024-01-15T...'
}
✅ User created successfully!
✅ Created user data verified!
1 passed (0.6s)
```

## 💻 Code Example 3: Negative API Test

```typescript
test('GET Request — User Not Found', async ({ request }) => {

    // Request a user that doesn't exist:
    const response = await request.get('https://reqres.in/api/users/999');
    //                                                               ↑
    //                                                    ID 999 doesn't exist!

    // Verify 404 status code:
    expect(response.status()).toBe(404);
    console.log('✅ 404 received for non-existent user!');
});
```

> 💡 **Negative testing for APIs = testing error responses!**
> Just like you tested invalid login in UI tests!

## 🔗 Combining API + UI Testing — A Real Pattern!

Here's a POWERFUL real-world pattern:

```typescript
test('API Login + UI Verify', async ({ request, page }) => {

    // STEP 1: Login via API (fast!)
    const apiResponse = await request.post('https://reqres.in/api/login', {
        data: {
            email: 'eve.holt@reqres.in',
            password: 'cityslicka'
        }
    });

    expect(apiResponse.status()).toBe(200);
    const { token } = await apiResponse.json();
    console.log(`✅ API Login successful! Token: ${token}`);

    // STEP 2: Use token for authenticated UI test
    // (In real apps — set the token as cookie/localStorage)
    console.log('✅ Ready for authenticated UI testing!');
});
```

> 💡 **Real-World Usage:**
> ```
> API test → Login and get token (fast!)
> UI test  → Use token to skip login UI (faster tests!)
> ```
> This makes your UI tests MUCH faster!

---

## 📊 API Testing vs UI Testing

| Aspect | UI Testing | API Testing |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| Speed | 3-10 seconds/test | 0.1-1 second/test |
| Browser needed | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Tests | User interface | Business logic |
| Stability | Can be flaky | Very stable |
| When to use | User flows | Data validation |

---

## ⚠️ Common Mistakes Beginners Make

❌ **Mistake 1: Not checking status code**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — only checking body, not status!
const body = await response.json();
expect(body.name).toBe('John');
// What if server returned 500 error with error message in body?

// ✅ CORRECT — always check status first!
expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
const body = await response.json();
expect(body.name).toBe('John');
```

❌ **Mistake 2: Using `--headed` for API tests**
```
// ❌ Unnecessary — no browser needed!
npx playwright test api.spec.ts --headed

// ✅ Correct — no browser flag needed!
npx playwright test api.spec.ts
```

❌ **Mistake 3: Hardcoding expected values without checking API docs**
```typescript
// ❌ WRONG — assumed wrong value!
expect(body.data.email).toBe('john@example.com');
// Actual email is different → test fails!

// ✅ CORRECT — check actual API response first!
// Use Postman or browser to check real response
// THEN write your assertion!
```

# 🔍 Found the Issue! — 401 Unauthorized Error!

Look at your error:
```
Expected: 200
Received: 401
```

> 💡 **Status 401 = "Who are you? Show me your ID!"**
> `reqres.in` recently updated their API to **require an API key!**
> Your request has no API key → Server rejects it → 401!

---

## 🌍 Real-World Analogy: A Security Guard 👮

```
You walk into a building:
Guard: "Do you have an ID card?"
You: "No"
Guard: "Access DENIED! 401!"

With API Key:
You: "Here's my ID card!" (API Key in header)
Guard: "Welcome! 200 OK!"
```

---

## ✅ Two Solutions — Pick One!

---

### Solution 1: Get Free API Key from reqres.in (Quick Fix!)

**Step 1:** Go to `https://reqres.in/`
**Step 2:** Click **"Get API Key"** → Sign up free
**Step 3:** Copy your API key
**Step 4:** Add it to your requests:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const API_KEY = 'your-api-key-here';  // ← paste your key!

test('GET request - GET USER DETAILS', async ({ request }) => {

    const response = await request.get('https://reqres.in/api/users/2', {
        headers: {
            'x-api-key': API_KEY    // ← Add API key here!
        }
    });

    expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
    console.log(`Status code: ${response.status()}`);

    const body = await response.json();
    console.log('Response body:', body);

    expect(body.data.id).toBe(2);
    expect(body.data.email).toBe('janet.weaver@reqres.in');
    console.log('✅ User data verified!');
});

test('POST request - CREATE USER', async ({ request }) => {

    const response = await request.post('https://reqres.in/api/users', {
        headers: {
            'x-api-key': API_KEY    // ← Add API key here too!
        },
        data: {
            name: 'Abiram',
            job: 'Automation Engineer'
        }
    });

    expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
    console.log(`Status code: ${response.status()}`);

    const body = await response.json();
    console.log('Created user:', body);

    expect(body.name).toBe('Abiram');
    expect(body.job).toBe('Automation Engineer');
    expect(body.id).toBeDefined();
    console.log('✅ User created and verified!');
});
```

});

## 📊 What is a Header?

```typescript
// Headers = extra information sent with the request!
// Like showing your ID card before entering!

const response = await request.get('https://...', {
    headers: {
        'x-api-key': 'your-key',           // API Key
        'Content-Type': 'application/json', // Data format
        'Authorization': 'Bearer token123'  // Auth token
    }
});
```

> 💡 **Common Headers:**
> | Header | Purpose |
> |--------|---------|
> | `x-api-key` | API authentication key |
> | `Authorization` | Bearer token or Basic auth |
> | `Content-Type` | Format of data being sent |
